source_title: Cassava Production Guide — Tanzania, East Africa

chunks.text: Cassava varieties for Tanzania: Cassava (Manihot esculenta) is the second most important food crop in Tanzania after maize. Improved varieties: Kiroba (bitter type, high yield 15-25 tons fresh root per acre, tolerant to cassava mosaic disease, 12-18 months to maturity), Mkuranga 1 (sweet type, 10-15 tons per acre, 10-12 months, good for fresh consumption), Albert (bitter, high starch content 25-30%, 15-20 tons, 12-15 months, good for flour and industrial processing), Nachinyaya (sweet, early maturing 8-10 months, 8-12 tons, good for chips). Local varieties: numerous local selections, variable yield 5-10 tons per acre, long maturity 12-24 months, often preferred for taste but susceptible to diseases. Bitter vs sweet: bitter varieties contain higher cyanogenic glucosides (require processing before eating), sweet varieties have lower levels and can be eaten fresh after cooking.

Cassava planting guide for Korogwe: Planting material: use stem cuttings 20-25cm long from mature healthy plants (8-12 months old), cut at 45-degree angle, 5-6 nodes per cutting. Planting time: beginning of long rains (March-April) is optimal, can also plant at start of short rains (October-November). Spacing: 1m x 1m (4,000 plants per acre) for maximum yield, or 1m x 0.5m (8,000 plants per acre) for faster ground cover and weed suppression. Planting depth: bury 2/3 of cutting in soil at 45-degree angle, leaving 2-3 nodes above ground. Soil requirements: well-drained sandy loam, pH 5.5-7.0, cassava tolerates low fertility but responds to fertilizer. Fertilizer: apply 50 kg DAP per acre at planting (place in planting hole), top dress with 50 kg CAN at 3 months. Cassava is drought tolerant once established but yields are significantly reduced by prolonged drought during first 3 months after planting.

Cassava pests in Tanzania: Cassava green mite (Mononychellus tanajoa) — feeds on undersides of young leaves causing leaf curling, yellowing, and reduced growth, most damaging in dry season, control: introduce predatory mites (Typhlodromalus aripo — biological control agent released in East Africa), spray with abamectin or sulfur. Cassava mealybug (Phenacoccus manihoti) — sucks sap from growing points causing stunting, leaf distortion, sooty mold, control: release parasitoid wasp (Anagyrus lopezi — successful biological control across Africa), spray with dimethoate if severe. Cassava whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) — transmits cassava mosaic virus and cassava brown streak virus, causes sooty mold, control: remove infected plants, use virus-free planting material, spray with imidacloprid. African cassava hornworm (Ceratomia undulosa) — large caterpillars defoliate plants rapidly, control: hand-pick caterpillars, spray with Bt or lambda-cyhalothrin. Root mealybug (Stictococcus sjostedti) — feeds on roots causing yield loss, control: crop rotation, deep ploughing before planting.

Cassava diseases in Tanzania: Cassava mosaic disease (CMD) — caused by African cassava mosaic virus (ACMV) and East African cassava mosaic virus (EACMV), transmitted by whitefly, symptoms: leaf mosaic, leaf distortion, plant stunting, yield loss 20-90%, control: use CMD-resistant varieties (Kiroba, Mkuranga 1), use virus-free stem cuttings from healthy plants, rogue infected plants, control whitefly. Cassava brown streak disease (CBSD) — caused by Cassava brown streak virus (CBSV), transmitted by whitefly, symptoms: brown streaks on stems, root necrosis (brown corky rot), most destructive in coastal East Africa including Tanga, control: use CBSD-tolerant varieties (Albert, Kiroba), avoid planting in low-lying humid areas, harvest early before symptoms develop in roots. Cassava bacterial blight (Xanthomonas axonopodis pv manihotis) — angular leaf spots, wilting, stem cankers, spread by rain splash, control: use disease-free planting material, crop rotation, copper-based sprays.

Cassava harvest and processing: Harvest timing: sweet varieties at 8-12 months, bitter varieties at 12-18 months. Harvest when lower leaves yellow and fall, stems become woody, tubers easily detached from stem. Harvest method: cut stem at 30cm above ground, dig around tuber with fork or hoe, lift carefully to avoid breaking tubers. Process immediately after harvest — cassava deteriorates within 2-3 days of harvest due to post-harvest physiological deterioration (PPD). Processing for bitter varieties: sun-dry chips (chop into thin slices, dry on raised racks for 3-5 days until crisp), or ferment (soak peeled roots in water for 3-5 days, then dry or mash), or roast (cook in fire to reduce cyanide). Flour production: peel, wash, grate, press to remove juice, sieve, dry in sun for 2-3 days, mill to flour. Fresh cassava storage: wax (coat cut ends with wax) and store in cool place for up to 2 weeks, or leave in ground and harvest as needed. Dry chips storage: store in bags in dry ventilated area for up to 12 months. Cyanide safety: bitter varieties contain 100-500mg HCN per kg fresh weight, processing reduces to <10mg/kg safe level.
